Social Democrats win supporters when they talk bluntly, boldly & passionately about practical issues that are important to average Americans: health care, affordability, opportunity, human rights & dignity, and reversing the imbalance in who partakes in America’s wealth – issues that had been core to the Democratic Party since FDR’s New Deal, but which many voters feel the mainstream Party now only gives lip service to. We can & should use Thanksgiving & the Fourth to teach young Americans that their country is a land of ideals, that Americans have accomplished much in pursuit of them, but – as fallible humans - have also fallen short, sometimes shockingly so; however, our greatness lies in our ability to admit that & try to do better.

comments.body: The WSJ piece is a good example of how easily readers can be manipulated by a frightening statistic stripped of its economic context. Ultra-low mortgage rates in 2020–21 pulled housing demand forward, while the subsequent surge in rates sharply worsened affordability and financial pressure across the housing market, so some deterioration in delinquency among newer and weaker borrowers should hardly be surprising. More importantly, UWM originates largely standardized mortgages that are sold into the agency market, with the overwhelming majority ultimately transferred to Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, or Ginnie Mae structures rather than retained as speculative credit bets on UWM’s balance sheet. That securitization system exists precisely to turn mortgages into investable, cash-flow-producing securities and keep capital flowing back into housing, a core pillar of American homeownership and household wealth creation. Framing that mechanism simply as a billionaire making “risky bets” backed by taxpayers turns a complicated housing-finance system into a partisan morality play, which may be entertaining, but is not at all illuminating.

For the recount, geographers used advanced mapping technology and cross-referenced with past aerial photos. I'm an appellate lawyer. At an ABA Appellate Summit meeting maybe 15 years ago, Justice Thomas explained to attendees his approach to questioning.

When he was a baby lawyer in Missouri, he nervously prepared for his first appellate argument, worrying about what tough questions he'd get from the court. But the judges on the court allowed him to make his argument without a single interruption. He was so grateful to them that, when he became a jurist, he resolved to treat lawyers that way. That's why he didn't interrupt lawyers at the lectern for years; he figured he was being kind to us.

I'll fast-forward and turn from history to inference: When SCOTUS adopted the current your-turn-next setup in 2020, he asked questions like any other member of the Court. That's because he wasn't interrupting anyone; this was his time, set aside for him.

The irony of this is that every experienced appellate advocate earnestly *wants* to be interrupted. We want to know what's bothering Justice X about our argument, so we can address it. The only lawyers who rejoice when they get no questions are neophytes who are scared to be at the lectern in the first place.

comments.body: I photographed the 2024 eclipse in Dallas TX. I prepared for months. I got good photos which I see daily hanging in my home. What was special is that 2024 was long enough to both catch the photos and just stand in awe of the universe.

comments.name: Cleon
comments.body: I have been under totality at three solar eclipses 1963 in central Maine, 1978 near Hood River Oregon, and 2024 in Northern VT.  Clouds cover ended our view of the sun in 1978, although it certainly became quite dark, and birds sang as some brightishness returned.  In Orgeon, I was entirely taken up with photographing totality and the diamond ring effect using a Linhof Supertechnica.  My reasoning followed the author here, so I did not bring a camera to the Vermont eclipse; and I certainly absorbed much more of the experience that way.  I recommend it.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
You did good, especially for a first-timer!  

I've photographed two solar eclipses, in 1970 and in 2017.  The first was with my new SLR camera using Kodak Plus-X B&W film and homemade solar filters from fogged film (state-of-the-art back then!).  I didn't know enough to remove the filter during totality, so the total shots were blank but the partial shots were terrific.

The second was using my cheapo Canon Powershot digital camera, using homemade filters using mylar solar filter sheets.  This worked much better and I knew to remove the filters for totality.  I switched to video mode for the final few minutes before totality so I have sound, too.

Gotta say, the best part is people's reactions as the sun goes out in the middle of the day.  For the first one someone nearby kept chickens and the rooster crowed.

comments.name: Joshua Murdock
comments.body: You absolutely nailed it, but that's no surprise for one of the best photojournalists out there. You consistently make incredible photos. I've photographed multiple full and partial solar eclipses for news orgs and I agree strongly with your final statement: Next time I will not be looking at it through a camera.

comments.name: Louis Giokas
comments.body:
Training an issue? What a crock. I mean that is the stupidest thing I have ever read in terms of electronics assembly. 

Who do you think Foxconn has assembling iPhones in China? It is peasants. I mean that literally. I knew this but it really was emphasized when, during COVID, there was a scare at one of their plants. A big outbreak. The government tried to keep the people locked in, but many broke out anyway. They hitched rides or walked back to their villages. There were lots of videos.

My younger son, in his early teens, built a gaming computer. He researched and ordered the parts and then he assembled it, in the family room, during Christmas when some of the parts arrived. It was very high performance. It even had liquid cooling for the CPU. He wanted to do it on his own, so I mostly watched. The only thing I helped with was installing the radiator for the cooling system. It was like working on my old British sports cars and motorcycles, drilling into metal to install a new part. The radiator even looked like a miniature car radiator. 

Training is required for any factory. There is no standard design. These are not consumer goods. So, anyone telling you training is a big deal for these companies is gaslighting you.
